provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Surah Al-Mulk part 1
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to recite Surah Al-Mulk verses 1-15.
The pupils should be able to explain the meaning of Allah's kingdom.

Introduction:
Last term we learned about the importance of reading the Quran. Today we will start learning Surah Al-Mulk which speaks about Allah's power and the signs in creation.

Content:
Surah Al-Mulk means 'The Kingdom'. It has 30 verses. We will learn the first 15 verses. 'Tabarakalladhi biyadihi mulku' means 'Blessed is He in whose hand is the kingdom'. This shows Allah controls everything. The sky, the earth, and all living things belong to Allah. When we see a big tree or the River Niger, we remember Allah's power.

Class activity:
Pupils will take turns to recite the first 15 verses of Surah Al-Mulk.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the meaning of Surah Al-Mulk?
2. Who has the kingdom according to verse 1?
3. How does this surah make us feel about Allah?

Summary:
Surah Al-Mulk teaches us about Allah's power and control over everything.

topics.title: Surah Al-Mulk part 2
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to recite Surah Al-Mulk verses 16-30.
The pupils should be able to explain how we can reflect on Allah's creation.

Introduction:
Last week we learned the first part of Surah Al-Mulk. Today we will complete the surah and learn about reflecting on Allah's creation.

Content:
Surah Al-Mulk continues by describing how Allah preserves creation. 'Allahu la yamutu' means 'Allah does not die'. We see Allah's signs in nature-the harmattan wind, the yam plant growing, the market full of people. When we see these things, we should think of Allah's greatness. The surah ends by saying people will be questioned about their lives on earth.

Class activity:
Pupils will draw three things from nature that show Allah's power and write how they make them feel.

Evaluation questions:
1. What happens to Allah according to verse 26?
2. Name two signs of Allah in creation.
3. Why should we reflect on Allah's creation?

Summary:
Surah Al-Mulk teaches us to think about Allah's power in everything we see.

topics.title: Hadith studies
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to state two selected hadiths.
The pupils should be able to explain how to live the sunnah in daily life.

Introduction:
Last term we learned about the life of Prophet Muhammad (SAW). Today we will learn some of his sayings and how to follow them.

Content:
A hadith is a saying of Prophet Muhammad (SAW). One hadith says 'The best among you are those who learn the Quran and teach it'. Another says 'Cleanliness is part of faith'. We can follow the sunnah by being honest in the market, helping our neighbors, and reading Quran daily. When we cook jollof rice, we can share with others like the Prophet did.

Class activity:
Pupils will write one way they can follow the sunnah at home and at school.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is a hadith?
2. State one hadith about learning.
3. How can you follow the sunnah when buying things in the market?

Summary:
Hadiths guide us to live good lives like Prophet Muhammad (SAW).

topics.title: Fiqh: purification
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to list the steps of complete wudu.
The pupils should be able to explain the importance of taharah.

Introduction:
Last term we learned about the five pillars of Islam. Today we will learn about purification which is necessary for salah.

Content:
Taharah means cleanliness. Wudu is the washing for prayer. To do complete wudu, we wash hands to wrists, rinse mouth, clean nose, wash face, arms to elbows, wipe head and ears, then wash feet to ankles. We must use clean water. If water is not available, we can use clean sand called tayammum. When we do wudu properly, our prayers are accepted.

Class activity:
Pupils will demonstrate the steps of wudu in pairs.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is taharah?
2. List three parts of the body we wash in wudu.
3. Why is wudu important before prayer?

Summary:
Proper purification makes our prayers acceptable to Allah.

topics.title: Fiqh: salah conditions
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to list the conditions of valid prayer.
The pupils should be able to identify mistakes in salah.

Introduction:
Last week we learned about wudu. Today we will learn what makes our prayer valid and acceptable to Allah.

Content:
For salah to be valid, we must have wudu, face the qibla, cover our awrah, have intention, and pray on clean ground. Awrah for boys is from navel to knees, for girls is entire body except face and hands. Common mistakes include talking, laughing, or not concentrating. When we pray in the mosque, we should not look around at others. We should focus on Allah.

Class activity:
Pupils will role-play salah and identify mistakes made by their classmates.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is awrah for a boy?
2. Name two conditions of valid prayer.
3. Why should we concentrate during salah?

Summary:
Prayer has conditions that must be followed for it to be accepted by Allah.

topics.title: Seerah: the early years
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to describe Prophet Muhammad's childhood.
The pupils should be able to state lessons from his early life.

Introduction:
Last term we learned about Prophet Muhammad's birth. Today we will learn about his childhood and the lessons we can learn from it.

Content:
Prophet Muhammad (SAW) was born in Mecca. His father died before he was born. His grandfather and uncle Abu Talib took care of him. As a child, he was honest and kind. He was called 'Al-Amin' meaning trustworthy. He helped his uncle with sheep. Even as a boy, he hated idols. We learn to be honest like him, help our families, and stand against wrong things.

Class activity:
Pupils will write one way they can be like young Muhammad in their daily lives.

Evaluation questions:
1. What was Prophet Muhammad's nickname as a child?
2. Who took care of him after his father died?
3. What lesson can we learn from his childhood?

Summary:
Prophet Muhammad's childhood teaches us honesty, kindness, and standing for what is right.

topics.title: Seerah: the revelation
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to narrate the story of the first revelation.
The pupils should be able to explain the importance of seeking knowledge.

Introduction:
Last week we learned about Prophet Muhammad's childhood. Today we will learn about how he received the first revelation from Allah.

Content:
When Prophet Muhammad (SAW) was 40, he used to pray in the Cave of Hira. One day Angel Jibril came to him and said 'Iqra!' which means 'Read!'. Muhammad said he could not read. Jibril hugged him tightly three times and then recited the first verses of Surah Al-Alaq. This was the beginning of Quran. This teaches us that seeking knowledge is very important in Islam.

Class activity:
Pupils will draw a picture of the Cave of Hira and the first revelation.

Evaluation questions:
1. Where did Prophet Muhammad receive the first revelation?
2. What did Angel Jibril say to him first?
3. Why is seeking knowledge important in Islam?

Summary:
The first revelation began the Quran and teaches us to always seek knowledge.

topics.title: Islamic economics basics
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to explain what halal earning means.
The pupils should be able to give examples of honest trade.

Introduction:
Last term we learned about zakat. Today we will learn about how Islam teaches us to earn and trade honestly.

Content:
Halal earning is money earned in ways allowed by Islam. We should not steal, cheat, or sell things like alcohol or pork. Honest trade means giving fair price and good measure. When we buy rice in the market, we should check the weight. A trader should not put stones under the scale to cheat customers. The Prophet said a truthful trader will be with the prophets on the Day of Judgment.

Class activity:
Pupils will role-play a market scene showing honest and dishonest trade.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is halal earning?
2. Give an example of something not halal to sell.
3. Why is honest trade important in Islam?

Summary:
Islam teaches us to earn and trade in ways that please Allah.

topics.title: Islamic history: Hijrah
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to narrate the story of the Hijrah.
The pupils should be able to explain the sacrifice made for faith.

Introduction:
Last term we learned about Prophet Muhammad in Mecca. Today we will learn about his migration to Medina which is called Hijrah.

Content:
The Hijrah was the Prophet's migration from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE. The Muslims in Mecca suffered from persecution. Allah told them to migrate. The Prophet hid in a cave on the way. Abu Bakr was with him. When the Quraysh reached the cave, they saw a spider web covering the entrance and a bird nesting there, so they thought no one was inside. The Hijrah marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar. Muslims left their homes, property, and friends for their faith.

Class activity:
Pupils will write a short paragraph about what they would take if they had to migrate for their faith.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is Hijrah?
2. How did Allah protect the Prophet in the cave?
3. What sacrifice did Muslims make during Hijrah?

Summary:
The Hijrah shows the sacrifice Muslims made for their faith.

topics.title: Revision and recitation
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to recite Surah Al-Mulk.
The pupils should be able to answer questions about term's topics.

Introduction:
This week we will revise what we learned this term and have a Quran recitation competition.

Content:
We learned Surah Al-Mulk, hadiths, wudu, salah conditions, Prophet's life, and Islamic economics. Let's review: Surah Al-Mulk teaches about Allah's kingdom. Wudu is necessary for prayer. The Hijrah was the Prophet's migration. We should earn halal money and trade honestly. For the competition, each pupil will recite Surah Al-Mulk from memory.

Class activity:
Quran recitation competition where pupils recite Surah Al-Mulk.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the main theme of Surah Al-Mulk?
2. Name two conditions of valid prayer.
3. Why is Hijrah important in Islamic history?

Summary:
We reviewed our term's learning and practiced Quran recitation.
